text:
alisa: Quick sketch — thinking about a hierarchical token/leaky-bucket that ties org and API-key limits directly to GPU pool capacity. Want quick feedback before I write a design doc. TL;DR: per-org bucket + per-key child buckets; both leak. Refill rates are dynamic based on pool utilization so we naturally backpressure when GPU pools saturate. Goals: fairness across orgs, predictable bursts, cheap graceful degradation (fallback to sparser models), and simple operational metrics.

matt.p: huge :+1: on tying to pool util. couple quick concerns: how do we handle cross-pool orgs (multi-region)? and burst accounting when requests are routed between pools?

kenji: agree with alisa. proposal for refill math: refill_rate_org = base_rate_org * (1 - pool_util) * pool_capacity_weight. child_key_refill = refill_rate_org * key_weight / sum(key_weights). Example: if pool_util=0.8 we scale down to 20% of base.

kenji: code sketch:```
// per-second tokens added
org_refill = base_org_tokens * max(0, 1 - pool_util)
key_refill = org_refill * (key_weight / total_key_weight)
```

diane: two operational notes: 1) tokens must be reserved atomically to avoid races — use Redis LUA or a small CAS loop in the admission service. 2) clock skew -> use monotonic counters for leaky bucket timing, not wall clocks.

rachel: metrics we need: org_tokens_available, key_tokens_available, blocked_reqs/sec, avg_queue_ms, model_fallback_count, pool_util_by_region. If we expose those as per-org dashboards we can set SLOs per customer.

matt.p: also think about burst fairness over time. If one key burns a lot of org tokens, should we limit subsequent keys for same org? Maybe a global org cooldown window.

alisa: good point. can add a borrowed_token counter: child keys can borrow up to X% of org bucket for short bursts, then cooldown penalty reduces refill for borrower. keeps small clients from getting starved.

kenji: fallback policy idea: when pool_util > high_watermark (e.g., 90%) automatically route eligible requests to cheaper model variant and throttle higher-cost ops. Keep admission decision simple: ALLOW (consume tokens), QUEUE (short wait if tokens likely to refill within 200ms), FALLBACK (route to cheaper model), REJECT.

diane: impl detail — queueing in front of GPUs is tricky. prefer short in-memory queueing at the edge with a hard timeout; long queues overload network and proxy threads. 200–500ms seems reasonable. Otherwise return 429 with Retry-After and a metric for latency SLO analysis.

rachel: rollout plan: 1) sim harness using historical traces to tune rates 2) canary in us-west with 1% traffic; monitor blocked_reqs, fallback_count, avg_queue_ms 3) 10% with ops alerting 4) global.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: canary job created: hierarchical-rate-shepherd v0.1 -> us-west-1, traffic=1% (started).

alisa: thanks everyone — I'll turn this into a short design doc with the refill formulas, fallback states, metric list, and a small API for admission checks (checkAndConsume(org, key, cost, opts)). Assigning follow-ups: @kenji for math, @diane for atomic reservation impl, @rachel for metrics/dashboards. Back in ~24h with a draft. :rocket:
